extracted.intended_audience: public_relations professionals / communicators pitching investigative reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Best-practice guidance for writing and delivering press releases and pitches aimed at investigative journalists, emphasizing verifiable evidence, sources, documents, and relationship-building rather than promotional announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive, reliable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide substantive, reliable information rather than hype or thin announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative reporters need material with depth — facts, data, and documentation they can build a probe around. Avoid lightweight promotional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure sources have credibility and can be relied upon by reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named sources who are willing to go on the record increase a pitch's usefulness; cultivate sources over time to build credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Make claims verifiable with documents or other primary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide internal documents, primary records, or pointers to documents so reporters can confirm facts; label provenance and how to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story leads, not announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitch should present a lead for investigative reporting rather than a promotional announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on narrative hooks, patterns, or unexplored angles that justify a reporter digging deeper rather than an event-style press release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust-based relationships / build relationships long-term
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop long-term, trust-based relationships with investigative reporters rather than only contacting them when you need coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meet reporters in person, have informal coffee meetings, and be a steady, reliable contact. Don’t only appear during crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over hype
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize factual substance (data, documents, sources) over promotional language and marketing spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer 'never before shared' exclusives, hidden angles, and evidence of patterns rather than flashy copy. Reporters value patterns and systemic issues over single-event PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch format for investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Format pitches to be less promotional and more document- and source-rich.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include background materials, offer source contacts, provide a timeline of events, attach or link documents, and use anonymized examples where appropriate. Keep promotional language minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard data
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply hard data that supports the story claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach or link datasets, spreadsheets, CSVs, or statistics reporters can analyze; raw data increases story-worthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary / internal documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide internal documents or other primary records rather than summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal memos, emails, reports, contracts, and other originals help reporters verify and build a story; label documents and explain provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower-quality information (when applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliver information of the kind a whistleblower might provide when appropriate and safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure protections for sources, consider anonymization, and provide corroborating evidence so reporters can assess credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named sources willing to talk / on-the-record access
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and offer named sources who are willing to speak on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters often require on-record or confirmable sources; offering access increases the likelihood of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry patterns / systemic issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Show patterns, trends, or systemic issues rather than isolated events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how multiple data points or cases fit into a broader pattern to support investigative angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrongdoing or misconduct revealed
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that reveals potential wrongdoing, misconduct, or regulatory failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports exposing malpractice or illegal behavior are high-value; ensure allegations are substantiated with evidence or documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest / clear public benefit framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the information in terms of public interest and clear public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the story matters to the public, regulators, or policy, and what the societal impact is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability and FOI/document-search accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Make claims verifiable and indicate whether materials are searchable via FOI or public records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State how documents can be corroborated (e.g., FOI-able records, searchable databases) and provide guidance on how reporters can confirm details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context (history, comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include contextual information such as history, comparisons, or benchmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context helps reporters understand significance — historical background, comparative data, and industry norms are useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply a clear timeline of events relevant to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chronological sequence helps reporters verify dates and causal relationships and anchors the investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish facts from interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly separate verifiable facts from interpretation, opinion, or spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label assertions vs. evidence so reporters can assess what is supported vs speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest about organization’s stake
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose the pitching organization’s stake, conflicts, or incentives honestly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters expect transparency about who benefits and any potential biases; hiding stakes undermines trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge complications / competing views
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge complexities, caveats, and alternative explanations or competing views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing counter-arguments or known limitations shows credibility and helps reporters anticipate rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer exclusivity for major stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer exclusivity (or label exclusivity) on major stories when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusives can entice investigative outlets, but be explicit about terms and time windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give reporters time to investigate properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow reporters reasonable time to investigate rather than demanding immediate coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be patient and responsive; investigative stories often take days or weeks to confirm and report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest answers to tough questions
rubrics_metrics.description: PR contacts should answer journalists’ difficult questions candidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid evasive or misleading responses; reporters expect straightforward replies and will note stonewalling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make documents available, not just summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the underlying documents rather than only summarizing findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summaries are less useful; attach or link to the original documents so reporters can evaluate and quote them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: Boilerplate releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sending boilerplate or templated releases that add no investigative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic press releases signal marketing motives and reduce interest from investigative reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: Marketing copy presented as news
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not disguise promotional marketing language as newsworthy information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative journalists quickly discard pitches that read like adverts; keep promotional claims out of investigative pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: Hiding key facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not withhold important facts or try to obscure damaging information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding facts reduces trust and can derail the relationship with a reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: Off-the-record after pitching
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid promising off-the-record information after making a pitch that appeared on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing terms (e.g., offering information then declaring it off-the-record) is a trust-breaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: Stonewalling on follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not stonewall or refuse follow-up information requests from reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be responsive to follow-ups; stonewalling signals unreliability and can prompt adversarial reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: Threatening legal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from threatening legal action to suppress reporting during or after a pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threats deter reporters and damage relationships; legal concerns should be raised carefully and transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: Astroturf campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid orchestrating fake grassroots (astroturf) campaigns or manufactured public support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Astroturfing undermines credibility and can be exposed by investigative journalists.
